title_en: God Is Worshipped Only by What He Has Prescribed
body_ar:
ذكرتم في محاضرة سابقة أنه من الفهم الصحيح للإسلام أن لا يعبد الله إلا بما شرع أريد توضيحا لذلك و هل يدخل في ذلك الأوراد المأخوذة عن الأشياخ؟ بالنسبة للعبادة نحن نعلم أننا نريد بها التقرب إلى الله تعالى و التماس مرضاته و في معاملتنا مع الأشخاص الذين يمكن أن نتقرب إليهم بما لم يأمرونا به لأننا نعلم ما ينفعهم و يضرهم مثلا هذا الشخص أعلم أن هذا الأمر ينفعه أو أن هذا الأمر يضره فأقدم إليه ما ينفعه و أدفع عنه ما يضره دون أن أستأذنه أو آخذ رأيه فهذا مما يتقرب إليه به

لكن الله تعالى يقول: «يا عبادي إنكم لن تبلغوا ضري فتضروني و لن تبلغوا نفعي فتنفعوني» فلا يمكن إذن أن نتقرب إليه إلا بما شرع لنا لأن ما لم يشرعه لا يمكن أن يكون فيه تحصيل منفعة له و لا دفع ضرر عنه وبسبب ذلك لا يمكن أن نعبده إلا بما شرع بالنسبة للأوراد هذه يتناولها عموم الأمر بالذكر في قول الله تعالى: (اذكروا الله ذكرا كثيرا) (اذكروا الله كثيرا لعلكم تفلحون) فأصلها جائز و مأمور به شرعا و كل شخص مأمور بكثير من الذكر و رسول الله صلى الله عليه و سلم كان يستغفر في الجلسة الواحدة أكثر من مائة مرة و لكن تحديد وقت معين أو هيأة معينة أو أسلوب خاص بهذه الأذكار فيه ابتداع من جهة و لذلك ينبغي أن يترك ذلك الابتداع و أن يأخذ الخير الموجود في الذكر.
body_en:
In an earlier lecture you mentioned that it belongs to a correct understanding of Islam that God is not to be worshipped except by what He has prescribed. I would like an explanation of that. And do the litanies (awrād) taken from the shaykhs come under it?

As for acts of worship, we know that what we intend by them is to draw near to God, exalted, and to seek His good pleasure. In our dealings with people, we can draw near to them by something they have not commanded us to do, because we know what benefits them and what harms them: this person, for instance — I know that such and such a thing benefits him, or that such and such a thing harms him, so I bring him what benefits him and keep from him what harms him, without asking his leave or taking his opinion; and that is among the things by which one draws near to him.

But God, exalted, says: 'My servants, you will never attain to harming Me so as to harm Me, and you will never attain to benefiting Me so as to benefit Me.' It is not possible, then, for us to draw near to Him except by what He has prescribed for us, because what He has not prescribed cannot contain any securing of a benefit for Him or any warding off of a harm from Him. For that reason we cannot worship Him except by what He has prescribed.

As for these litanies, they are covered by the general command to remember God in the words of God, exalted: {Remember God with much remembrance} (Sūrat al-Aḥzāb 33:41); {and remember God much, that you may prosper} (Sūrat al-Jumuʿah 62:10). So their basis is permissible (jāʾiz) and is commanded in the revealed law, and every person is commanded to a great deal of remembrance. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, would ask forgiveness more than a hundred times in a single sitting. But the fixing of a particular time, or a particular arrangement, or a manner peculiar to these remembrances — there is innovation in that from one angle. So that innovation ought to be left, and the good that is in the remembrance taken.

flags.arabic: لكن الله تعالى يقول: «يا عبادي إنكم لن تبلغوا ضري فتضروني و لن تبلغوا نفعي فتنفعوني»
flags.context: the pivot of the whole argument, introduced as 'God, exalted, says'
options: render in quotation marks as reported divine speech, not in Qur'anic braces
render in the curly braces used for Qur'anic quotation
flags.note: IMPORTANT. The Sheikh introduces this with 'God, exalted, says', but it is not Qur'an: it is a ḥadīth qudsī, divine speech reported by the Prophet, from the well-known report of Abu Dharr. House style reserves the curly braces for Qur'an, and using them here would present a hadith to English readers as a Qur'anic verse. It has therefore been set in ordinary quotation marks. The Sheikh gives no narrator, collection or grading, and none has been supplied.

flags.arabic: فيه ابتداع من جهة و لذلك ينبغي أن يترك ذلك الابتداع
flags.context: the Sheikh's verdict on fixing a time, form or manner for the litanies
options: 'there is innovation in that from one angle … that innovation ought to be left'
'that is an innovation … it is obligatory to abandon it'
'that is a forbidden innovation which must be given up'
flags.note: EDITORIAL REVIEW, AND A RULING-STRENGTH FLAG. The Sheikh is careful in three ways that an English rendering can very easily destroy. He says there is innovation in it 'from one angle' (min jihah), not that the practice is innovation; he uses yanbaghī, 'ought', not yajibu, 'is obligatory'; and he explicitly affirms that the basis of the litanies is permissible and commanded, and tells the questioner to take the good in them. The Arabic is a qualified and largely conciliatory answer about a practice associated with the Sufi orders, and it has not been hardened. Given the subject, the publication decision belongs to Ummah Collective and the Sheikh's office.

options: the litanies (awrād) taken from the shaykhs
the devotional formulae received from spiritual masters
the wird practices of the Sufi orders
flags.note: The questioner means the fixed daily litanies transmitted within the Sufi orders, which in the Mauritanian setting is a live and sensitive matter. Option 2 makes explicit what the Arabic leaves implicit, and option 1 is nearly a transliteration. The middle course taken here keeps the Sheikh's own level of explicitness; the reader is not told more than the Arabic tells them.

translator_notes: The date carried here is the CMS record date. Across this whole slice the site serves a bulk-upload timestamp of 19-21 December 2010, which is when the written archive was loaded into the site, not when the Sheikh gave the answer or delivered the lecture. date_is_cms_upload is set true. The real date of composition is not recoverable from the page and has not been guessed.
Qur'anic and hadith renderings in this file are interpretive translations of meaning, offered to carry the Sheikh's argument in English. They are not a substitute for the Arabic.
The question and the answer run together in the source without a break; paragraph breaks have been introduced in body_en for readability, and body_ar is left as the source has it.

The two Qur'anic quotations are given in the source in round brackets and without references; the references have been supplied per house style. The second matches Sūrat al-Jumuʿah 62:10; the same wording occurs at Sūrat al-Anfāl 8:45 with a different opening.
'Innovation' renders ibtidāʿ, the verbal noun, which the Sheikh uses here rather than bidʿah; the glossary entry for bidʿah applies.
jāʾiz is used here in its ordinary legal sense, 'permissible', not in the creedal sense of rational possibility covered by §8 of the style guide.
